answer.rationale:
Only two of the five candidate directions actually resolve continuity: the primary contract lapses in 14 days and does not auto-renew, so add_second_source and defer_decision would leave the line — already at 94% of committed volume with zero buffer — without a qualified primary. That narrows the real choice to renewing/negotiating with the incumbent or switching wholesale to the low-cost vendor.

The memory that would justify switching is memory_c2, so that is the one I spend my single verification pull on. It is the load-bearing claim under the cheapest-looking path and it is the most likely to be misapplied: it is a year old, and the record as consolidated does not say which component class it covered, at what share of volume, or whether the vendor was ever run at full committed volume rather than a partial award. 'Onboarding was quick and invoicing stayed accurate' is evidence about administrative fit, not about sustained delivery reliability at 100% of a line with no buffer — those are different failure modes, and the consolidation may have smoothed that distinction away. If the archived record shows the switch was a full-volume primary award in a comparable category, switching becomes the defensible answer and I will revise; if it was a partial or non-critical award, memory_c2 does not support betting an unbuffered line on it.

Pending that, I intend negotiate_terms, guarded. The incumbent has refused to reopen price this cycle, but memory_c4 (benchmarking moved both price and payment terms) and memory_c6 (term structure unlocked volume pricing without narrowing scope) point to levers other than a straight price reopen — term length, volume tiers, payment timing. I keep this small rather than locking a long multi-year commitment: a shorter benchmarked bridge preserves the option to qualify the low-cost vendor as a second source at the next review (memory_c3's pattern), whereas a multi-year lock would forfeit exactly the leverage the 18% mandate needs.

Explicit residual risk: negotiated terms alone may not reach the full 18% cut, and I am not claiming it will. The downstream risk of the alternative is worse and less reversible — a mid-cycle delivery miss at 94% utilization cannot be undone by a later review, while a cost shortfall can be closed next cycle by dual-sourcing. I am trading a quantified probable cost gap against an unquantified continuity failure, and I would rather carry the gap. Confidence is moderate precisely because it hinges on what the memory_c2 archive shows.
